detail in the X6’s shot, and the highlights are also preserved slightly better. Similar to the X5,
the Osmo360 can also have issues with lens flares in certain situations—and in this comparison,
you can see that the X6 handles lens flares significantly better than the Osmo360.
There’s one important topic we haven’t even touched on yet: Just like the Osmo360, the X6
can shoot in 8K at up to 50 frames per second. The X5 offers a maximum frame rate of 30 frames per
second in 8K. This is a significant upgrade, especially for those who prefer a slightly
smoother, more natural look. On the other hand, I’m a bit disappointed with the 360 slow-motion
footage. The X6 shoots in 4K at up to 100 frames per second, just like the Osmo360. The X5 is the
only one of the three cameras capable of shooting in 4K at 120 frames per second. On top of that,
I find that the X6’s image quality in 4K100 isn’t optimal, and that the X5, in particular, produces
better slow-motion footage in 4K. We’ll see that, fortunately, when it comes to slow motion, the X6
has a significant advantage in Single Lens mode. And the X6 has another feature that’s been long
overdue for Insta360. It supports 10-bit Log recording, even in 8K. The X5 does have a LOG
color profile, but only in 8-bit. Furthermore, the X5’s LOG profile isn’t available in 8K—only
in 5.7K. The Osmo360, on the other hand, also features a 10-bit Log profile that lets you
shoot in 8K. However, this is D-LOG M, and as you can see here, D-LOG M is nowhere near as flat as
the X6’s new Log profile. As a result, the dynamic range of the X6’s Log profile is better than that
of D-LOG M on the Osmo360. I converted these two clips using the manufacturers’ LUTs, and
unlike the Osmo360, the X6 produces a very neutral image that’s well-suited for further processing.
But the X6 has another important advantage when it comes to color profiles. It’s the first 360 camera
capable of capturing 8K 360 footage in 10-bit HDR Dolby Vision. This means footage where,
in particular, the highlights can be displayed much brighter. To take advantage of this, however,
you’ll need an HDR-capable display, such as the screen of a modern smartphone or a modern TV. As
you can see here in this direct comparison, the HDR footage has significantly more contrast and
looks more realistic. As my YouTube review isn’t an HDR video, I can’t show the full
dynamic range. But I get the impression that HDR videos sometimes look a bit overexposed,
even when viewed on a smartphone. Insta360 could do with making some improvements in this area.
You can reframe your 360 Dolby Vision video as usual and export it as an HDR Dolby Vision video.
This is a great feature for anyone who frequently watches their videos on a smartphone or TV.
The X6 has also made slight improvements in low-light performance. The X6 is the
best 360 camera to date for shooting in low light. Similar to the X5 and the Osmo 360,
it has its own dedicated shooting mode for use in low light. However,
the difference compared to the X5 isn’t that big. Especially considering the size of its sensor,
the X5 already takes very good shots in low light. It’s also extremely dark here. Actually,
you shouldn’t really be filming in such lighting conditions. But this scenario is
simply better suited for comparison shots and to better highlight the differences. As I said,
the difference compared to the X5’s footage really isn’t that big. The X6’s footage has slightly less
image noise and is a bit sharper. And here, too, you can see that the issues with lens flares have
been resolved. The same applies when compared to the Osmo360. The Osmo360’s footage is darker and
lacks some detail. As mentioned at the beginning, the Osmo360 has sensors the same size as the X6.
This means that the performance of the Pure Video mode is simply the deciding factor,
as was also evident from the X5’s good results. But you can’t say that the X6’s lead is huge.
Interestingly, the differences in Single Lens mode are perhaps greater overall than in 360
mode. The X6 clearly performs better here. This is true both when compared to the Osmo360 and
when compared to the X5. The colors in the X6’s recordings look better, and they also show more
detail. And that brings us to a topic where the X6 has made great progress: the single-lens mode.
As we’ve just seen, the X6 clearly performs best in low-light conditions among all three cameras
in Single Lens mode. But that’s not the only improvement Insta360 has made in Single Lens
mode. All three cameras can capture flat footage with just one lens, which you no longer need to
reframe. And just like the Osmo360, the X6 can now also capture flat footage in 5K at up to 60 frames
per second. On the X5, the maximum is 4K60. As you can see here on the camera, with the X6 you can
set the field of view relatively freely in Single Lens mode and also enable distortion correction.
That’s really cool – the footage in Single Lens mode looks good, but I’ve also noticed that the
Osmo 360 and the X5 apply more HDR processing. The highlights can blow out a bit more quickly
on the X6 in Single Lens mode. I don’t know if that might change with a future firmware update.
what I’m really excited about is that with the X6 in Single Lens mode, you can now also shoot
slow-motion footage in 4K at up to 120 frames per second. This is also possible with the Osmo 360,
but only in the extremely wide ‘Boost’ mode. With the X6, 4K120 is available in Single
Lens mode regardless of the field of view. This means the X6 is increasingly capable of
replacing a traditional action camera. High-quality slow-motion footage has
been one of the few remaining exclusive features of a standard action camera.
Of course, all three cameras still have several other shooting modes, such as for time-lapses
or hyperlapses. Just like the Osmo360, the X6 can take 360 photos with up to 120 megapixels.
I’ve done a comparison of a few photos here in the office, as many people are interested in
indoor 360° photos. This is a heavily cropped version of the photos. Unlike the Osmo360,
the X6 has a significantly higher dynamic range, also because it features an HDR mode. The level
of detail is also slightly better than on the Osmo360. Compared to the X5, there’s a
noticeable improvement in detail, partly because the X5’s photo has significantly fewer megapixels.
There have also been improvements to the Bullet Time mode. The Bullet Time mode is
now available for the first time in 8K at up to 100 frames per second. But I find
the Instaframe mode—which is exclusive to the X6 and X5—much more interesting. In Instaframe mode,
you can select a subject and track it directly in the camera, much like you would with a gimbal
camera. You’ll then get a perfectly reframed flat clip in 4K with the “Invisible Selfie
Stick” effect. No more editing required. The tracking and reframing are therefore performed
directly in the camera. If needed, you can also simultaneously record a 360 backup clip in 8K,
which you can reframe yourself—just in case you’re not satisfied with the flat clip.
Simultaneous recording in 4K and 8K—that’s not possible with the X5. When recording a
flat clip and a 360 clip at the same time, the resolution on the X5 must be reduced to 1080.
And that brings us to a topic that sets the X6 and Insta360 apart. The goal is to increasingly
relieve users of the need to edit and reframe their footage. After all, reframing is still
considered the biggest drawback of a 360 camera. To take the reframing off the user’s hands, the X6
supports a new, completely revamped Autoedit feature in the app. You select a few clips,
and the app does the rest. Until now, the results were rather average. That has now actually been
improved. By the way, the intro clip was created using the new Auto Edit feature.
But there are two more new features. With the new AI Director feature,
the X6 analyzes all clips recorded that day at the end of the day and while charging,
identifies highlights, and automatically transfers a custom-generated daily vlog to
your smartphone—all fully automatically—you don’t actually have to do anything except activate the
feature. Everything runs on the camera and app. No upload to the cloud is required for this feature.
With AI Director, you don’t even have to select the clips yourself. This feature automatically
compiles a montage of some of the best shots of the day, which you can share straight away.
In contrast, the new cloud features, Moments & Moments Pro, which work in conjunction with Google
Gemini, are quite different. After you’ve uploaded your clips to the cloud, Moments Pro becomes a
kind of personal editor. The clips are analyzed, and various editing schemes are suggested. You
can then select different tags or protagonists and start the edit. This process takes place entirely
in the cloud, and you’ll be notified as soon as the video is ready. The feature is interesting and
works well, but there’s a catch—you’ll naturally need a cloud subscription to take advantage of it.
depending on the keyword, it can also pick out key scenes from older,
perhaps even forgotten, recordings. All three features represent an upgrade
to the previous AutoEdit function. Generally speaking, in my opinion, it’s not about getting
the best possible result from your footage. Rather, it’s about getting a good montage of
your footage quickly and easily, without having to do the editing yourself if you don’t feel
like it. And the results can be really cool! But that isn’t a feature exclusive to the X6.
all the new automated editing features will also be available for the X5. If you’d like to find
out more about the new Autoedit features, have a look at my tutorial on the subject.
I’ll include a link to it in the description. With all these new features and the smaller
form factor, the question of recording time naturally arises. So how long can the X6 shoot,
and are there any overheating issues? I ran a test here in the office at 8K30 at
a warm 26 degrees Celsius and without any airflow. Under these unfavorable conditions, there were no
overheating issues whatsoever, and the X6 was able to shoot for an incredible 2 hours and 38 minutes.
That’s 1 hour and 10 minutes longer than the Osmo360 and the X5. Only the X5 had overheating
issues under these conditions and shut down after 56 minutes due to overheating. Of course,
it’s worth noting that in real-world use and with airflow, none of the three cameras will have
overheating problems. For most people, overheating will therefore remain more of a theoretical issue.
But Insta360 has gotten everything right this time when it comes to overheating and battery life.
To capture shots like this one or this underwater shot, a 360 camera requires
very specific accessories. And in this regard, not only the X6 but also the X5 have a major—if
not decisive—advantage. It’s true that all sticks and mounts are compatible with all 360
cameras. But Insta360 is the only manufacturer so far to offer an Invisible Dive case for its
360 cameras. And only with such a dive case can you take 360° shots underwater, since underwater
shots place entirely different demands on lens stitching. Unfortunately, the Dive Case for
the X6 wasn’t available at the time of my test, which is why you’re seeing footage from the X5
here. But a Dive Case for the X6 will be available soon. However, a dive case is now also available
for the X6. Apart from that, there are several remote controls, ND filters and other special
mounts and accessories available for the X6. And have you seen this: the Luna Ultra’s POV
Head Tracker? It’s worn like a headset and is also compatible with the X6. When using the
Instframe mode, The framing automatically adjusts to the movements of your head.
Personally, I wouldn't want to do without the DiveCase. For me personally,
the lack of an Invisible Dive Case is one of the Osmo360’s major weaknesses
I know that many users aren't particularly interested in audio quality. But Insta360 has been
constantly working to further improve the audio quality of its cameras—and the X6 is no exception.
The X6 features a new Windproof 360 microphone. The camera has microphone openings on all sides
that are protected from the wind. And of course, the X6 also includes the excellent
Voice Enhancement mode, which effectively filters out background noise. But of course,
for even better audio quality, there are external microphones available for all
three cameras. The best choice for the X6 is definitely the relatively new Mic Pro.
What else is important? What other differences are there between the three cameras? The X6 also
comes with a very special feature: 3D Spatial Capture. Put simply, this is a technique that
creates a 3D model from a video or photo – a 3D model within which you can move around freely.
This is a particularly important upgrade for anyone who uses their 360° camera professionally,
for example for virtual tours. You don’t just get a photo where you can look around freely;
you get a high-quality 3D model in which you can move around freely. For example,
a house that you can explore virtually and freely. For many people, this is certainly a very cool
feature. Unfortunately, 3D Spatial Capture is not available in the US at launch for technical
reasons. However, this is set to change. And for me, very important:
Unlike the X5, the X6 finally has internal storage. At 47 gigabytes, it’s only about
half as much as the Osmo 360, but it’s enough in case you forget your SD card. And, of course,
the apps are important, too. Especially when compared to other manufacturers, the Insta360 apps
are still the best in terms of feature set. This applies to both the smartphone app and the desktop
app. That said, you can of course also reframe your clips quite well with the DJI Mimo app.
I think the X6 has turned out to be a fantastic camera that gets almost everything right. And
the new AutoEdit features and 3D Spatial Capture expand the functionality of a 360-degree camera.
Of course, that comes at a price. The Insta360 X6 starts at $699 in the U.S. and at €699 in Europe.
That’s the only real downside of the X6 in this comparison, since the X5 is already available
starting at $550 or €590 in Europe. The Osmo360 is similarly priced, but you can find it cheaper from
third-party retailers like Amazon. You’ll find links to all three cameras in the description
below. If you use the link for the X6, You'll also receive an exclusive creator gift pack. It's
supposed to be an extremely useful Double Lens KIT that lets you replace two damaged lenses.
So check out the offer—it's a limited-time deal, so you'll want to act fast if you're interested.
If you have an older camera, there’s also a trade-in program you can take advantage of. This
applies to DJI and GoPro cameras as well. I’ll include a link to this in the description too.
So what would I recommend? In my opinion, the X6 has turned out to be a perfect 360 camera. It has
hardly any flaws, and aside from slow-motion in 360 mode, there’s hardly anything more you could
ask for right now. I really like the new lenses and the fact that all the lens flare issues have
been fixed. The new automated editing options are cool, too. It’s basically a flawless camera,
though it doesn’t have any absolutely standout killer features. If you’re buying a new camera
and can afford it, I’d go with the X6. But if you want to save some money, the X5 and the Osmo360
are still very good alternatives. Give me a like as feedback if you found this video interesting.
A detailed beginner’s tutorial on the X6 will follow soon. So stay tuned, and see you next time.

heart rate, and power to your cycling
videos? It's very simple. This is how I
do it. I use a Insta360 GO 3S or any
Insta360 camera and a COROS Dura bike
computer. I start the Insta360 GO 3S
recording from my phone to have precise
timestamps and simply record the ride on
the COROS Dura computer. When you're
finished, open up the Insta360 app, go
to the clip you want, select stats,
stats source, COROS, and bam, magically
all these stats will appear. Super easy
and seamless and your video is ready to
be posted with all these overlays.

caption_lines.text: So, the X5 is Insta360's flagship

which one should you buy? I've tested

to help you decide. And honestly, the
results might surprise you. And just so
you know, this video is completely
unsponsored. All of my gear reviews are,
honestly, all of my own thoughts. So,
first off, let's talk about the image
quality, because that's obviously one of

the fact that this should have better
image quality than the Ultra. However,
when I actually did side-by-side tests,
so I actually rigged up these two
cameras next to each other and went out
and filmed, when I matched the shots in
post, the Ultra came out looking better
every single time. As you can see from
these shots, everything looks sharper.

range. And this applied no matter which
mode I was in, both in 8K on the X5. And

there is one huge caveat. In order to
match the field of view on the GO Ultra,

footage. And so, naturally, this meant
that I lost a lot of resolution and a
lot of detail. However, when I exported

from the X5, in my view, the footage
looks just as good, if not better, than
the GO Ultra, with colors looking really
natural, really bright and vibrant. And
especially in the 8K mode, everything
looks really sharp and really crisp. And
also, not over-sharpened, and I really
like. Now, for me, this really starts to
get at kind of the key difference
between these two cameras, and that is
kind of the obvious thing that the X5 is
a 360° camera, while the Ultra is more
of a standard single point of view
camera. And so, what this means in
practice is that the X5 is constantly
having to expose for the entire
environment, which is a lot harder to
do. Whereas, with the Ultra, it's only
exposing for where you're pointing it.
So, if you're pointing it at a bright
light source, it's going to expose for
that. Whereas, if you point it at
shadows, it's going to expose for the
shadows. Whereas, with the X5, it has to
expose for everything all at once. And
in my experience, I would say that when
you factor this in, I think the X5
actually does perform better. You also
have to consider the fact that even when
you're in 8K mode, if you're cropping in
on an 8K resolution image that's a full
360° view, you're going to lose
resolution fast. So, it's really hard to
compare the image quality side by side
in that regard, because while with the
Go Ultra, you're getting 4K in a single
specific field of view, on the X5,
you're splitting 8K across two sensors
that are getting a full 360° field of
view. All that to say, really, at the
end of the day, I think, generally
speaking, you're going to get
better-looking images from the X5, but
it will be a wider field of view. If you
want a more standard field of view, and
you're okay with a slightly lower image
quality in general, then the Go Ultra
will do the job. Once again, this kind
of hints at a broader difference between
the two cameras, which I'll get more
into as we go through the video. So, the
next thing I wanted to talk about
briefly is the size and portability of
the two cameras. So, the X5 is the
biggest camera in the Insta360 lineup,
and the Go Ultra, outside of the action
pod, would be less than a third of the
size of the X5. Now, to me, that doesn't
mean that the X5 isn't portable, because
it really is. I can still definitely
pocket the X5 as well as the Go Ultra.
But, I think the thing you have to
remember with portability with the two
cameras is that the X5 really needs to
be used on a selfie stick. You have to
kind kind have it away from your body to
get the best images from it. If you have
it too close to yourself, you're going
to get a lot of distortion and warping.
So, you kind of have to factor in
carrying around a selfie stick with you
on top of the X5. With the Ultra,
because it's so compact and it's more of
a standard camera, you can get away with
filming without any sort of selfie stick
or tripod. And so, I would say this is
more truly pocketable than the X5. You
can also film quite easily just holding
it at arms length, and you can get some
really good results with it. But, of
course, you can also attach all of the
standard accessories with a quick
release mount on the bottom, including
selfie sticks and tripods. So, I think
in that regard, the Ultra probably wins
the portability battle. So, let's move
on to the battery life. And this one to
me has a pretty clear winner out of the
gate, and that is the X5. And that's
primarily because it's got a removable
battery. And that's despite the fact
that with the standard battery on the
X5, you actually get less record time.
So, shooting in 5.7K 30, the battery is
rated for 135 minutes. While you're
supposed to be able to shoot for 170
minutes inside the action pod in 4K on
the Ultra. However, the big benefit of
having a removable battery is that you
can have multiple batteries that are
fully charged, ready to swap straight
in. While on the Ultra, it's a fixed
internal battery. So, if you want to
charge it, you're going to have to plug
it in via USB-C. On top of that,
Insta360 also released an extended life
battery for the X5 called the Ultra
battery, which is kind of confusing.
But, with this extended battery, you can
get up to 235 minutes of record time.
So, just that battery alone is going to
beat performance of the Ultra. So, I
think if you're going to go on longer
shoots, going traveling with the X5, and
you can get your hands on a second
battery or the extended battery, then
that to me is why the X5 wins the
battery battle. Now, let's talk about
the next part, which is also a pretty
key difference, and that is workflow.
So, when it comes to shooting, this is
probably the biggest difference between
these two cameras. So, with the Ultra,
you really have to be quite intentional
about the shot that you're getting.
Because it's a single fixed point of
view, it's much more like a standard
camera in that regard. So, if I want to
be filming myself, I actually have to
turn the camera to myself, make sure I'm
getting a good angle by looking at the
preview screen, and then as I'm filming,
I just have to constantly quickly check
to make sure I'm still filming myself,
and then I've got the angle pointing in
the right direction. And this is totally
fine. Like generally, this is how you
would film with most cameras, whether
it's a huge mirrorless camera, a cinema
camera, point and shoot, whatever it is.
That's the standard way you would film.
The biggest benefit to this is that it
really forces you to actually think
about your shot while you're filming it.
And this could maximize your creative
results. So, you have to really think
about your framing while you're
shooting, make sure it looks good, make
sure you've got your exposure right, all
those sorts of things to help you get a
good shot in camera so that there's
minimal work to do in post when you take
it to your computer. Now, the negative
of this is that it's going to take you
out of the moment to some degree.
Depending on what you're doing, you have
to spend some mental energy thinking
about your shot, thinking about your
framing, making sure it looks good while
you're actually doing the filming. And
again, this could really suit you if you
really enjoy the process of filming, if
you like getting good shots. But if
you're doing something a bit more
action-oriented where you really prefer
to be in the moment and you don't want
to have to think too much about
capturing footage, this could be a bit
of a distraction. And that is really the
strength of the X5 because you really
just don't have to think about it when
you're filming with it. The only thing
you really have to spend mental energy
on is thinking about the height of the
camera. So, generally, I find holding it
at about eye level when I'm trying to
film myself is ideal. So, as long as I'm
keeping it at roughly about eye level, I
know that I'm safe and it's filming

I don't want the distraction of having
to think about my framing while I'm
skating. So, just being able to hold out
a selfie stick and really not think

downside to this is that you do have to
do more work in post. So, using either
the phone app or the desktop app.
Generally, with 360 footage, you have to
tell it where you want it to be looking.
For me personally, I actually find that
process quite fun. It's an enjoyable
process reframing my shots, so it's not
a huge burden for me. It might be
annoying for you, depending on which

Insta360 have also thought about this,
and the X5 now comes with a couple of
modes that help to minimize this
post-editing work, including a mode that

subject and will always keep you
centered in the frame. So, who is each
camera for, and then which is my
personal pick? I think if you're someone
who does a lot of action related stuff,
like sports, bike riding, skating,
anything that you really just want to be
focused in the moment and be able to

caption_lines.text: In this video I'm going to be giving you tips on shooting 360 travel videos.
Everything from how to shoot your footage, the best accessories,
as well as tips on capturing unique and creative-looking angles.
Hey everyone, Steve here from Learn Online Video
and today we're talking all about how to capture creative and unique-looking travel videos using a 360 camera.
Now I recently flew out to Stockholm, Sweden
and this was my first YouTube networking event.
I was really looking forward to exploring the city and meeting creators from all over the world,
but I didn't want to be the guy staring through the lens of a camera the whole time.
I didn't want a camera strapped around my neck,
I didn't want to have to think about things like framing, composition, focus, exposure,
but I did want to document the trip,
and this is where a 360 camera comes in.
These things are small, discreet, easy to travel with and make capturing your footage incredibly easy.
So let me share with you some tips to help with your own travel videos when using a 360 camera.
Now the camera I used on this trip was the Insta360 X3.
This one's great because it shoots in 5.7K and it's got a nice big screen
so you can easily change all the camera settings without having to connect it to your phone.
Now there are four accessories which I think are almost crucial when it comes to shooting 360 travel videos.
Number one - the Invisible Selfie Stick.
This will be magically erased from your shot and is great for capturing both yourself and your location.
Number two - a mini tripod.
This will steadily hold both your camera and your Invisible Selfie Stick, comes in really useful.
Number three - a Suction Mount.
This will allow you to attach your camera to just about any flat surface.
And finally number four - a clamp for whenever you can find a nice flat surface to attach your camera to.
Now how you shoot your travel video and the footage you capture is entirely up to you.
Do what works best for the story that you're trying to tell.
For me, I wanted to capture shots not only of my destination but also my journey to that destination.
You could for example capture a POV shot whilst you pack your suitcase,
or you could capture a timelapse as you drive to the airport.
Now the Invisible Selfie Stick comes in very useful at the airport
because it's easy to carry with your luggage and folds down nice and small when not in use.
It also allows you to capture shots as you walk through the airport from multiple different angles
and this gives you a good variety of footage to work within the edit.
Also, try getting creative with your shots and angles - I clamped my camera to the bottom of my suitcase for this shot,
and sent it around the conveyor belt for this shot.
Now once you've boarded the plane and taken your seat don't feel like there's no longer anything to shoot
because there is literally a whole window of opportunity to take advantage of.
Shooting in timelapse mode as the plane takes off.
This is a great way of adding more pace to your travel videos.
If time lapses aren't your thing then try shooting in real time.
Also experiment with your framin in the edit.
The beauty of shooting in 360 is that you can point the camera wherever you like.
You could point it towards you, you could zoom right out and get really creative,
or you could turn the camera facing out the window.
The possibilities are endless.
Now this 360 camera comes with an app that has a ton of features and effects
which makes shooting and editing your footage much easier.
For example, this shot here was captured by me simply walking around the airport -
I just selected the Cinelapse feature in the app and the editing software did all the rest.
I was also able to edit this on my phone whilst at the airport,
so when you combine the 360 camera with the app you get the ultimate power combo when it comes to travel videos.
Now when I arrived in Stockholm I really wanted to explore the city,
and in Stockholm there really isn't any better way to explore the city than on an electric scooter,
and this is where the 360 camera really came to life.
And what I love most about shooting in 360 is that the camera is shooting in every single direction,
so you don't need to think about your framing or your composition whilst filming.
You can enjoy whatever it is that you're doing and then reframe all of your footage later in the edit.
There are an infinite amount of shots that you can get when shooting in 360.
As an example here is the exact same shot edited three different ways:
Edit number one - facing forward, camera locked off, nice and simple,
similar to what you might capture using a more traditional camera.
Edit number two - exact same shot only this time we're going to tilt down as we push forward to reveal the road ahead.
And edit number three -
let's get much more creative with this one, consistent camera movement that creates a much more immersive experience.
So quite often deciding the framing of your shot is the most difficult part because there's so many options.
Also, don't always feel like your camera needs to be moving.
You could place it still on a table during a meal for example and then get creative in the edit later.
Now whilst I was traveling in Sweden I was trying to travel light.
I didn't have my laptop with me, so I was editing everything on my phone.
I used a feature on the Insta360 app called Auto Frame which quickly and easily reframed my footage using AI.
This is a great feature, especially for beginners who are new to editing.
Editing 360 footage is made so much easier using the app because of all the effects that can be easily added.
What used to take days, weeks of editing on a computer now literally takes seconds on a phone.
This sky replacement effect for example would take a huge amount of time back in the day,
but now with just one tap of a button - voila!
Also if you're looking for more control over your edit and a higher-resolution export
then this is where the Studio app comes in.
I use this when editing on a laptop as I can create much more technical and precise camera movements.
The app is a great, quick, on-the-move way to edit your footage
and the Studio app on a computer is better when editing bigger projects.
This tutorial here for example, the video that you're watching right now,
I edited my 360 footage on the Studio app here on my laptop
and then imported it into my editing software for the final edit.
So look I feel like we're just scratching the surface of 360 travel videos here,
but hopefully, this is giving you a few ideas for your own travel videos.

I fully extended the selfie stick behind me,
then slowly brought the selfie stick up and over in front of me to reveal the waterfall.
To edit the shot, I will put myself in the middle,
pinch my fingers to zoom out and add a keyframe,

add a keyframe,

Shot number five is the bumper shot.

I mounted the three suction cups on the car,
extended the selfie stick by two stems,
pointed the selfie stick in the air and drove for at least two minutes.
To edit the shot, first I will go to Settings and turn on Direction Lock,
next I will add speed, so I will go to Tools,
Speed, select 4x speed.
Then I'll put the car in the middle,
add a keyframe, and finally, I'll go to Tools,
Motion ND and turn it on,

Shot number six is the timelapse.

then I will move the view to the left,
add a keyframe, use the Dewarp field of iew to zoom in,

add a keyframe,
and now when I play it back I have a timelapse shot.
